text:
Jacek Karpiński was born in 1927 in Turin, Italy, into a family of Polish intellectuals and alpinists. His father, Adam Karpiński, was an aeronautic engineer and inventor, while his mother, Wanda Czarnocka-Karpińska, was a respected physician. After his father's death in 1939 during a Himalayan expedition, Karpiński continued his education and joined the Gray Ranks, a Polish underground paramilitary group, where he served in assault units. During World War II, he was injured while working on homemade bombs, losing sight in both eyes and facing a hand amputation, though he recovered fully. He later participated in the Warsaw Uprising, where he was trapped and wounded, remaining paralyzed after the conflict.
After the war, Karpiński moved to Radomsko and completed high school, later attending the Faculty of Electro-Mechanical Sciences in Łódź, graduating in 1951. He worked at the Polish Academy of Sciences' Institute of Basic Problems, where he designed the AAH—Analytical Analyzer of Harmonics, a device that improved weather forecast precision by 10%. In 1959, he co-developed AKAT-1, the world's first differential equations analyzer based on transistors, praised for its aesthetic design and technical innovation.
Following a successful scholarship in the United States (1960), Karpiński returned to Poland and designed the Polish perceptron, a device capable of recognizing shapes and objects, one of the first of its kind in the Communist bloc. In 1965, he developed KAR-65, a fast, asynchronic computer with a dedicated operating system, used in scientific data processing. Despite its technical excellence, the project failed to achieve mass production due to political resistance and lack of industrial support.
Later, Karpiński moved to the countryside and worked on Nagra tape recorders in Switzerland. In the 1990s, he advised on computer science and attempted to launch business ventures, including a handheld text-scanner and cash registers, both of which failed. He was awarded the Officer's Cross of Polonia Restituta in 2009 and posthumously received the Commander's Cross in 2010. Karpiński died in 2010 in Wrocław. He is also known for his controversial work as a secret informant for the Służba Bezpieczeństwa, where he collected technological data, a practice that sparked historical debate over the scale and impact of his engineering achievements.
